utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A minor transcript point to start the day on the first line, 12th of February perhaps. Good morning, Mr. Sakic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your cross-examination by the Prosecutor will now continue. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth continues to apply to your evidence today, as it did yesterday. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. The two vehicles that you travelled to Kosovo in, the two Puh vehicles, you called them, were they marked or unmarked police vehicles?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These vehicles were blue. They also had rotating lights on them and it didn't say "police."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wasn't there a danger at that time in travelling in a convoy of this nature? Weren't NATO planes in the air?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's why -- can I actually provide an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is why we were careful in terms of keeping our distance during this transport. When there were woods, we went closer; through towns we went closer to each other; and on open roads we kept a longer distance, a distance between vehicles, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the occasion that Protic travelled to Kosovo with you in the same vehicle, you're in a Toyota motor vehicle, unmarked Toyota motor vehicle? I will give you the licence number shortly. In any case you were in an unmarked Toyota vehicle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. May I explain that as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. You have said you were not -- you didn't travel in an unmarked Toyota vehicle. Did an unmarked Toyota vehicle accompany at any time on any of these trips to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some questions briefly about these places that you mentioned. When you went to Janjevo did you meet the police who were there?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we came to the centre of Janjevo, that's where the patrol was waiting for us, and they took over. I didn't get out of the vehicle at all. Protic told me that he was going with them. He said that through the window. He said that he was going with them and that we should wait for him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I just --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't talk to that patrol at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I just wanted to know precisely, you didn't meet or speak with him. So you do not know the names of those police officers who went for those bodies or went with Protic to get those corpses?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that shipment, so to speak, you escorted it to Petrovo Selo in the northern part of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the other shipments of dead bodies that you escorted, you left Mr. Protic with the cargo on the road; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were given an assignment to escort Protic and his cargo and you ceased escorting them before they reached the destination on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you got your instructions to escort the corpses and Protic, were you told where you would escort them to?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. I was told that on that day I would be working with Mr. Protic and that I would receive further instructions from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, now you're taking it a little bit further because I think I'm now hearing that you were told that you received instructions from him. So you are saying you were told to escort Protic and his cargo and Protic told you when to stop escorting him? I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for all further instructions, we gave them all from Protic once he took us over or we took him over.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task was only to escort him from point A to point B and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So on one occasion he took you to the place where the bodies were deposited, that was Petrovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not to the place where they were deposited. They went over the hill. I didn't go all the way with them. We only came to the gate and I stayed there. They went up there on their own and I don't know what happened up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if we could, with your leave, go into private session because I saw from the document that when this aspect was dealt with in the court in Serbia they went into private session because names of senior individuals were mentioned. I assume that they had reason to do it there, and to be quite frank, they didn't actually go into private session, they just referred to people by numbers, but it's impossible to do that here. So I would ask if we could go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is because you're going to refer to particular names?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what basis do you have for saying that by conducting the evidence in public they will be exposed to any danger?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I believe that -- and my conclusion is based on what happened in the record I'm seeing of the interview in Serbia, that he referred to certain persons by numbers on a photograph. Now, I don't know if it was because of a security reason, but I do recall that Mr. Protic had -- on at least one occasion was asked about this particular place, had said one of the reasons why he was afraid to name names was because persons would know that he named their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're saying that the issue is the safety and security of Protic rather than the individual that may be named?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not the individuals who are named. It's the safety and security of this witness and Protic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you object to that course of action?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would leave this to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a situation where we are satisfied there is enough information to justify going into private session for the security of persons who feature in this trial. However, should any party consider, having heard the evidence, that it's inappropriate that the evidence remains private, then it's open to that party to make a motion to us to make the record of the evidence public. We'll now go into private session. 21 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by later order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you gave your statement to the police, this was in respect to an investigation of the mass grave at Petrovo Selo, that's your statement in 2006.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is what they were investigating, they were investigating the other mass graves, they were investigating your other trips and they were investigating General Lukic's connection, if any?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think this might create some confusion because I think it's obvious through the statement we received from the Prosecutor yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Counsel is about to give evidence and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's clearly a matter that you could deal with in re-examination. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You went up to Petrovo Selo to a police training-ground which was in the vicinity of a park?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who were the policemen that you saw there that were involved in the reception of this consignment?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I knew one of them by his nickname, Djera. I was shown some photographs. I think I recognised a person who had the number 8 and I cannot recall whether there was some other photographs too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- were you told the name of the person with the number 8?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What name was that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I cannot remember. They showed it to me, but I think that they wrote something down there that they knew, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The chief -- or did you know the chief of the gendarmery in Kosovo at that time, Guri Radosavljevic or Goran Radosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of him, but I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was one of the persons that you identified as being there?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see him. Maybe he was there, but I didn't recognise him. Later on I saw him on television when he became a general, but I cannot remember him being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Arsenijevic, did you --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arsenijevic Milenko, if that's who we're talking about, I didn't see him, because I know him because he worked with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see the chief of the Kladovo secretariat of the interior, a man by the name of Sperlic, there?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sperlic is the name, I saw him, but not when we got there, only after about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I think we can come out of private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's obvious now that there was no need for this private session, so at this time we would object to have this part of the witness's evidence in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To hear further argument on that I'm afraid we would need to return to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no objections, then, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're content --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- this should be made public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. The evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The evidence will be made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the occasion you went to Kosovska Mitrovica where you went to the lumber shed you said -- you spoke about a captain of police telling you about bodies. What was the name of that captain?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the name. I think he worked in the Kosovo police. I don't know his name exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, as a lieutenant of police at the time, now that you have discovered for sure that you are involved in shipping bodies and you thought it important enough to make a report, a written report about it, you didn't get the name of the person who told you; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, at that time I didn't have time to learn all the details because the truck had already been loaded and Protic was about to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but this was one of the situations, according to your evidence, in which you had to wait around while they loaded bodies onto the truck, so that was naturally an occasion where you would have been standing around or sitting around for enough period of time for a lieutenant of police to find out some basic things like who are the people there. You did not -- you can name nobody who was there; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Earlier in your evidence yesterday you told us that you made a note in your notebook on some trip you went to that Sperlic had taken a spade from a van and put it in the truck --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I misspoke this name yesterday several times, it's not Sperlic; it's Protic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Thank you very much, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you said that with a straight face.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You noted that Sper -- sorry, withdrawn. You noted that Protic put a spade in his truck and you didn't note -- as a police officer you didn't note who were the people involved and who told you that they were involved in shipping dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Mr. Protic took a spade, when we were driving to Pristina, the first trip, not Kosovska Mitrovica, that's when he took the spade because there were two jeeps there, American made. And from one of these jeeps he took a spade and he put it into his truck, the one that he was driving, I think it was a Scania truck. As for the second truck that had been parked there, he took the tools, the jack, and so on, and other things that I could not remember, and I informed my superior officer about that in my written report. What he did, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And you also thought it fit at that time to write down those things in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so that I could write a report to my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you wrote a report to your superior about being told by senior policemen or a senior policeman that these were dead bodies you were carrying, and yet you didn't write in your report who was giving you that information -- or in your notebook? Anyway, I withdraw the question. Let's -- weren't there at that place, at that place in southern Kosovo, Mitrovica, more than one, several policemen from Serbia engaged in bringing and loading bodies?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I claim with full responsibility here in this place that there was no higher-ranking officer there from the MUP of Serbia except for the captain who was providing security there and there were three persons -- no, four persons in civilian clothing and about five or six policemen -- I mean I thought that those civilians were policemen too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it possible that the five or six persons in civilian clothes might have been policemen that you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. How could I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't five or six. There were five or six in uniform and four or five in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the first instance you testified about, how long did it take you to travel to -- I think it was -- let me see, the utility square in Pijaca -- public utility company at the square in Pijaca. From your departure point in Serbia to the public utility square where the truck was picked up, how long did it take you to travel?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we had set out around 1400 hours from Belgrade. We came to a town called Blace, that's where we spent the night, I and Mr. Stosic at Mr. Protic's house, and the other men spent the night at the hotel. Protic took them to a hotel that was nearby, only about 200 metres away. On the following morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you speaking now about the first time you went to Kosovo with Mr. Protic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I'm just asking you now from the departure point in Serbia when you set out --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- for Kosovo, how long did the travel last?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Kosovo and back you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to the place where you picked up the bodies, the square at Pijaca?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe about six hours, five to six.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What time did you leave the departure point to get to Pijaca?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Belgrade? From Belgrade, we set out at 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What time did you arrive at Pijaca?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, we spent the night in the town of Blace, and in the morning at 6.30 we set out and we came there at around 8.30, that's in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what time did you arrive at Velika Plana?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly, but I think it was in the afternoon, maybe sometime after 5.00 or 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long did it take you to travel there from Pijaca?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At around 5.00, we were not in any hurry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said at around 5.00. You mean you left for Velika Plana -- sorry. I'll ask the question again. How long did it take you to travel to Velika Plana from Pijaca?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you stop?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because we had stopped for maybe a minute or two, for the excavators to move away at the bridges that had been torn down. That was at the place called Rudare.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that was the only delay to Velika Plana at Rudare?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just for the trucks to pass. We stopped there for as long as it took them to move away and to enable us to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about Rilindja, when you picked up bodies or picked up the truck at the Rilindja parking lot, how long did it take you to travel from Rilindja to Velika Plana?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, something like that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Five hours.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What time did you arrive at Rilindja?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At around 1300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Rilindja, you said, is on the outskirts of Pristina or is it in Pristina itself?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is closer to the Caglavica-Kosovo Polje road, to the junction there, I think it's closer to that spot than to Pijaca. It's closer to the gas station where we had taken the turn than to the place where we had gone earlier where the market, pijaca, was. But I can't really say now because Prota would tell us, Go there, go somewhere else, but I was not really all that familiar with Pristina at all so he would just tell us where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're obeying Prota? You were obeying the instructions of Prota, I take it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's okay. That's right, that's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What time did you arrive in Velika --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, before you ask that -- what is Pijaca, is that a place?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Pijaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Pijaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Pijaca is a place he said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a market-place in any city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, that's what I'm understanding from the -- I don't think it's a village name or a place name, it's the market-place, as I -- It's coming over as pijaca in the Serb, which is obviously the same word as --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- in several languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What time did you arrive at Velika Plana from Rilindja?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the afternoon at around 5.00, 5.30 p.m., something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We now -- oh, yeah, that's clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just have a moment to check the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you arrived at Velika Plana at 8.30 in the morning. Yesterday you said you spent about 10 minutes there for Mr. Protic to pick up the truck, so we're talking about approximately 8.40 in the morning. You said it took you about five hours to travel from there to Velika Plana, but you also said that you arrived at Velika Plana at about 6.30 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you had left -- if you had spent only ten minutes in the place where you picked up the truck and travelled five hours without delay to Velika Plana, you would be at Velika Plana at about 1.30. According to what you are telling us, there are about four hours which are not accounted for. How do you account for those four hours?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I think that you're mixing up the first and the second trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first trip we arrived there at -- down there at around 8.00, 8.30 in Pristina and then we went to Velika Plana, it took us five hours. In the second trip we headed out on the same day from Belgrade and then we reached to Rilindja on the same day and back to Velika Plana, it took us about 10 or 11 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But, Mr. Protic [sic], the question I asked you was quite specific. How long did it take you from the public utility company pijaca, which I called Pijaca -- sorry, Mr. Sakic, so sorry. And you told us five to six hours you arrived there around 6.30 --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also told us yesterday that you spent about ten minutes to pick up the truck on that occasion and you told us this morning that you arrived there at 8.30 in the morning. I suggest to you that those four missing hours was --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- the time Protic used in Pristina to make his call, to make his phone call from a land-line. Do you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, please allow me to explain. I stand behind my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Protic did not use land-lines to phone, that's first thing. Second thing, we never spent more than ten minutes in Pristina. And the first trip we arrived -- we headed out for Pristina at 9.00 and -- or from Pristina at 9.00 and we arrived at Velika Plana at 1.00 or maybe 2.00 p.m., and it took us maybe one more hour to get to Belgrade from there, a hundred kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think now you realize the significance of it, I'm asking about the timing, you are telling us something entirely different in what time you arrived at Velika Plana. While you were in --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. The witness explained to the Prosecutor that he makes two trips. If he wants further clarification he can get it from the witness but he cannot draw the conclusions. He can pose the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think that's a matter for the Court from the record, if I may move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The objection is that you're making a statement rather than asking a question, so please ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On these trips that you made to Pristina and environs of Pristina, is it your evidence that Mr. Protic was within your line of vision at all times?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except at the last trip where he went with the local police into the mountains, but at all other times he was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm asking you about -- I'm just interested in Pristina, because it is my suggestion to you that it was at Pristina that he left you for a few moments to make a phone call from a land-line. Do you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It was insecure at that time, I think you would agree with me, for people engaged in military activities or any activity that they would want to keep secret to use cell phones to communicate, was it not, during the war?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Mr. Protic never did talk, except to give our location, over the mobile phone. He would just answer the questions giving our location, as far as I could hear. I couldn't of course hear what was being said at the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you will agree with me that for sensitive or secret operations the policy was to use land-lines?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, didn't you tell us that when Protic made a call or used a cell phone, you told him that he was going to give away your location?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no, in fact, I told him, Why are you revealing our location?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. So -- and you knew at that time in Kosovo there were specific land-lines dedicated for the use of the forces, the armed forces, the police and the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I knew was that there existed a special telephone line and just the usual telephone lines. I wasn't aware of any other kinds of phone lines, but that applied to the whole of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You retired -- to move on quickly, you retired in 2000 --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wasn't that early retirement?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a disability pension.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. What sort of disability you had?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had some problems. I had been in an accident, and a fungus moved in my eye, and also in my knee, the patella in my knee, had to be -- I had surgery in my knee and I could no longer perform the job that I had been in before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Police lieutenant, I've seen you walk in here, I've seen you look at stuff. Do you have a problem walking or do you have a problem with your eyes?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have problems with my right eye, and as far as my left eye is concerned, because of the strain, I'm also losing sight in that eye too. I can see up close but not at a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you have two apartments. When did you get ownership of your apartments?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't have two apartments. I have an apartment in Belgrade, 62 square metres; and I have a house in the village of Vladimirovac, that's in the Alibunar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did you get your apartment in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in 1990 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is where you were, you said, when you saw Proto, Mr. Protic, in 2005, you were outside your apartment?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Nikolaja Gogolja Street, the house number is 38A.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I understand from your evidence, and if necessary I'll read to you, that after the war you saw him then in 2005 outside your street, outside your house, and he said to you -- and you said, Proto, is that you? And he said, Yes, it's me, and then started an outburst against Lukic --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- saying that other drivers had gotten apartments, Lukic didn't give him any, and he was going to testify against Lukic. Now, why is it that this man would make this outburst to you in these circumstances if he did not know that you knew, you all knew, that all of you were mixed up in this transport of bodies? Why would he say that to you if you didn't know about Lukic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I need to give you a longish answer to that question. When I asked him how could he blame a man, I'm not trying to defend Lukic or anyone, I'm just here to tell the truth. So I asked him how could he blame a man whose name he never mentioned. He told me the following. During the war he was the tenth violin, and from the year 2000, the 5th October, he was the first violin. And he said that he had asked him for an apartment twice and he had not given it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is your explanation for this outburst to you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you very much. I have nothing further for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, what was the significance of the 5th of October, 2000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This date is significant because the democratic forces won in the Republic of Serbia, and there was a change in the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sakic.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the cross-examination we heard that you were the ranking officer at that trip. Were you able to influence the course of this trip in your capacity as the escort?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I was not in the position to influence it because Mr. Protic was my superior de facto. This actually went contrary to some of interpersonal relations because I was an officer and he was a policeman. But let me add, he was a trusted person of the person who had actually issued the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And is it also true or is it true, was he actually the person responsible for the task and you were just the escort?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was my task to provide security and escort to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who do you say he was the trusted person of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, whoever it was that issued the task to him, because he knew where he was going and what he was doing, and he would just show us where to go by switching on the indicator, you should turn left here, right there, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, that was a rather specific statement: "He was a trusted person of the person who had actually issued the orders ...", which sounded at first as if you knew who it was who issued the orders. Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who gave him the orders, but he had his superior officers who issued his orders and I had my superiors. Our units were separate units, and I was only providing escort. But it appeared that whoever issued orders to him did not trust me as the person who was in charge, who was in a position of -- in a managerial position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Until now I had understood that you acted as you did because you had been instructed by your superior to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My superior officer told me, You are to provide security to Bozidar Protic today, and he will give you further instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who gave you your instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of my unit, Colonel Mladen Sipovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that was the case on each of the four occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All four times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, what did you know about the previous duties of Protic prior to your first trip with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that he was a driver in the joint affairs administration and I knew that there were another six or seven drivers including Protic. I knew nothing more about him or them. I only knew what I knew about him when I travelled with him and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you learn from him who he had driven in that role, who of importance he had driven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't know. Perhaps he would drive occasionally all of the senior officers in MUP, but I didn't really know about that. He mostly drove trucks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did you know about his background in the police that led you to the view that he was a trusted person of whoever was giving directions on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that his father was in police -- at least he said something to that effect. So that's probably why his superiors trusted him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You travelled very close to him on four occasions over significant distances when communications took place between him and someone else, you stayed in his house, and you say that you still did not get any information to help you identify who he had spoken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was twice in his house. I stayed once overnight and on the second occasion I stayed outside of the house, had coffee there. I don't know who he talked to. All I know is that he said to me that he had talked on a mobile phone with Rodja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did he say that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He told me that in Pristina when we arrived in Pristina on the first trip at the market-place, that pijaca, because he was in the car behind me and I asked him. He avoided to answer. He was probably looking for an opportunity where the two of us would be alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this the first reference you've made in your evidence yesterday and today to Rodja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned him yesterday and I have mentioned him today as well. In the first trip and in the second trip he spoke twice on a mobile with somebody, and when I asked him about it, both times he answered that that was Rodja and that that was how he communicated with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may be of the assistance, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- I'll give you the line. Usually he mentioned the last name of this person but he -- and he would mention either the last name or the full name of this person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give me a reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's page 22.082, line 13, and on other places as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yours has been updated; mine has not. And how many pages into yesterday's evidence was that, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give us one second, please. Approximately the 58th page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's even the previous witness, I'm afraid, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know if I might be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- did a WordWheel search for the word "behind," you would find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's actually the 68th page, Your Honour, and it's line 25 now in the un-updated version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, why is it that you do not think that the person who trusted him was Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I didn't hear that and I can't tell you something that I didn't hear, didn't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend from the Prosecution asked you whether you were interrogated about Petrovo Selo when you were questioned at the police in Belgrade, and I will ask you this: On this occasion did you explain, did you tell them about all of these four trips to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as I have explained to you today and yesterday, that's exactly what I did there with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to your recollection, did you say to them exactly the same thing you said to us today?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you also mention Djordjevic in your statement to the police in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, without knowing that I would come here to the Tribunal to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, that completes your evidence here. Thank you for coming to give evidence. You may leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness is Mr. Miroslav Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have binders prepared for this witness the same way for the last one with clear documents, so if we could get some assistance from the usher and hand this to Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we commence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have your written statement as part of your evidence and we have your personal details and career details in that statement, but I would still ask you to introduce yourself to us.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I am Miroslav Mijatovic, born on the 2nd of November, 1951, in the village of Baijevac, Obrenovac municipality, and that municipality belongs to the territory of the city of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I started working at the police on the 1st of July, 1971, after completing secondary police school which lasted for four years, and I remained in the police force until I retired on the 31st of December, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, I'm just going to give this by way of a brief introduction so that we can understand the rest of your evidence, but the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija started becoming more complex in 1981, Albanians started leaving police force in 1990, as a result of which there was a shortage of policemen in Kosovo and Metohija. When did the situation in Kosovo and Metohija become extremely complex?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Starting in 1991 until 1997, we can say that that was a lull. The situation was somewhat calmer, but there was a danger of excessive situations arising on a daily basis. And then in 1997 the incidents of terrorism stepped up, became a daily occurrence basically. So that starting from that, time based on the information I have, there were 134 terrorist attacks in which 39 people were killed. That was in 1997. And then in 1998 there was an expansion in terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, and by way of illustration there were 2.010 terrorist attacks in which 328 persons were killed, if I remember the figures correctly, give or take two or three. Out of the 328 persons, 118 were policemen and additional 16 were kidnapped, which means that in comparison with the preceding seven years, the incidents of terrorist attacks increased by 50-fold, 1500 per cent and that was an increase -- and in terms of the persons killed, the number increased nine-fold, which is 903 per cent, and that briefly illustrates the situation in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 and explains the reasons for that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not dissatisfied with your answer, I'm just waiting for the interpretation to be completed and for the transcript as well, that's why I'm making a pause.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you something about the composition of the staff, that was a topic that interested both the Prosecution and the Chamber yesterday. When was the last time you were sent to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I was sent there last time in mid-July 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were the tasks that you performed during your last stay in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I was deputy commander of the staff of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, deputy head of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did your post terminate in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 31st of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who signed the decision sending you to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Chief of the public security sector, General Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under whose orders people came to the staff of MUP?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: All members of the staff came there pursuant to the orders of the senior officers of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for the composition of the MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija, did it change in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Members of the staff changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could head of the MUP staff affect that, influence that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no influence whatsoever because the decisions on sending people there were made either by the minister or heads of various sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could anybody else from the staff affect or influence the composition of the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody else whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that when you're deciding who's the best man for the job down there you don't take account of the views of the people on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no way we could decide on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but are you saying that the -- those in Belgrade with responsibility for determining who should be in the staff in Kosovo would not consult the top brass in the staff in Kosovo before making an appointment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to tell you whether they consulted anyone. I know that they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand that answer in the English translation. Could you give me it again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What I'm saying is whether they had any need to consult anyone and whether they consulted anyone else. All I know is that they did not consult me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but you're -- you're saying that it's not possible for someone who is in the staff, in particular the head of the staff, in Kosovo to have any influence on who's appointed there; and that seems very strange to me just from a common-sense point of view, that you would have such a system, you might send a man totally unsuited for the terrorist environment down to deal with terrorism because you hadn't, as a manager in Belgrade, checked up on what the particular issue of the moment was. And is that -- are you saying that's how things operated, there was no consultation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you once again, nobody consulted me about who should be sent by the leaders of the ministry down to Kosovo and Metohija. It was up to them to decide that. Now, as to whether they consulted anyone else on that issue, I really don't know about that. As for the staff, staff was unable to make a decision as to who was going to be the member of the staff. None of the staff members could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand -- that's easy to understand, but it's the idea that the head would have no influence at all on who might be appointed to his staff. That seems strange. However, let's proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could we please have P1505 in e-court now. We see this on our screens now, a decision on the establishment of a ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism, 16th of June, 1998, is the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult to follow this on the screen so we have prepared the document so that you could have it in front of you. So let's go through this name by name and could you tell us who the members of the staff were from this list -- or can you tell us in your day, let's deal with it that way, who were members of the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: In my day, to the best of my recollection, because that's not stated in the decision, in addition to General Sreten Lukic it was myself, then it was Dusko Adamovic, Goran Radosavljevic, Novica Zdravkovic, Desimir Slovic, Radovan Vucurevic. I don't know if I remembered everyone but I think that's it -- oh, yes, Milan Dzankovic. Dobrasin Krdzic and Mike Rajcic. I think I've mentioned all of them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would just like to go back to some of them. Do you know when Goran Radosavljevic was no longer on the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know he was no longer on the staff from the same day when I was no longer on the staff, namely, from the 31st of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 6D1045, not to open it again now. It is a decision on the secession of the appointment of Goran Radosavljevic. Do you know when Novica Zdravkovic was no longer on the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I think sometime in mid-February 1999, I think it was the 15th of February, around then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence Exhibit 6D1047.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Radovan Vucurevic was no longer on the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was terminated on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we've now lost P1505. Was that your intention, that we should be looking at something else? I thought you were avoiding opening these other exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm avoiding opening the other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So let's go back to P1505, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mijatovic, I interrupted your answer. You were being asked when Radovan Vucurevic's appointment was terminated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radovan Vucurevic was no longer on the staff from the 1st of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Dusko Adamovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: The first date -- the same date, the 1st of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to go back for a second once again. Radovan Vucurevic, 6D1049, that's the decision on the termination of his appointment and we don't need to have it open now. We still have to deal with Desimir Slovic. When was he no longer on the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Also as of the 1st of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were members of the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: According to the document in front of us, though, each member of the staff had a particular responsibility. What was the responsibility of Slovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was involved in analytical affairs on the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the names on the document in front of us is Dinovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Djinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Djinovic. Who held his position in the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Djinovic was not on the staff when I came there, and I do not remember in terms of decisions what duty he had on the staff. I think that he was the deputy there, but I'm not sure. There is a decision, as far as I can remember, on this but I'm not sure right now. I think he was the deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you were there, who was the assistant head for interventions and operational planning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, I see it now. I didn't pay attention to it. Yes. Now I see it, that Radislav Djinovic was assistant head for interventions and operational planning as of the 16th of June, 1998, that's the decision. However, when I got there, I didn't find him there. I cannot say specifically who it was that replaced him because work was done differently on the staff. There are other staff members here mentioned in the decision who were not there at the time when I arrived. I know that Adamovic was in charge of operational matters and that Radosavljevic was involved in training and equipping units, and of course Dusko helped with that, but Dusko was mainly in charge of operational matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So even the ones who are recorded on this list may have been doing different jobs by the time you were appointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Individuals were not there at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But, for example, Radosavljevic here is said to be the assistant head for police units, but you say he did a different job related to training.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, sorry, I do apologise, he's here towards the bottom here. I was looking at Djinovic. Oh, yes, yes, but he did work on training and equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mijatovic, now I would like to talk about people who were not members of the staff and who were nevertheless on the list of persons who are listed here as members of the staff in this decision. First of all I'd like to ask you about the following. We see in this decision that the deputy head of staff is David Gajic, that is what is written here. Was Mr. Gajic a member of the staff while you were on the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: That's what this decision states; however, throughout my stay there David Gajic was not a member of the staff at all, or rather, he did not do any work within the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just a moment. The decision doesn't say what the position was when Mr. Mijatovic arrived. He was not appointed, according to the evidence so far, until mid-July 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking him during his tenure whether he ever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but the answer's he's just given was -- your question: Was Mr. Gajic a member when you were on the staff, and his answer is: That's what this decision states, but it doesn't state. The rest of the answer is fine for our purposes, but it's important the witness understands that this is a decision that relates to a period a month before he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, it was my mistake, probably inartfully posed the question. I will be more precise in future. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to the activities of Mr. Gajic, there is a Defence Exhibit, 6D302, we are not going to call it up now. I would just like to state that for the record. I would like to ask Mr. Mijatovic the following: Who replaced Mr. Gajic in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I was sent to the staff of the Ministry of the Interior in Pristina. I told you already, I think it was the 15th of July when I arrived down there. I did not see Gajic on the staff, and I don't know whether I was the one who replaced him. At any rate, I was appointed deputy head of the staff, and he did not hand over any duty to me. I did see him in Kosovo, but I don't know whether he ever did anything on the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Once again, my mistake. I meant who replaced Mr. Gajic in terms of the office he held in the state security sector in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Gajic was replaced by Milisav Vilotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to Mr. Vilotic, there is a Defence exhibit, 6D303, and I would like to ask you, Mr. Mijatovic, whether Mr. Vilotic while you were in Kosovo was a member of the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here in this decision we see on page 1 the fourth person mentioned as a member of the staff is Milorad Lukovic, better known as Legija. Was Milorad Lukovic a member of the staff while you were on the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not. Milorad Lukovic, Legija, was not a member of the staff while I was on the staff. I did see him perhaps once or twice, I cannot say for sure, when he came to attend some meetings that were chaired by the minister, but that he was a member of the staff, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I should move slightly to another topic, so is it the appropriate time for the break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic, we have to have a break at this stage for a half an hour; while we have that break, would you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mijatovic, my colleague Mr. Ogrizovic from our team reminded me that I omitted a procedural matter. Can you find the written statement there that is 6D1492. Can you find it there? I think it was outside the binder.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I found it, 6D1492.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you were to be asked the same questions today, would you say the same things?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender Mr. Mijatovic's statement, the one that is 6D1492. Let's move on now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you do, just give us a moment. The copy I have, Mr. Lukic, has two page 4, and they are a little different. The problem surrounds paragraphs 9 and 10 I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know when I first received the statement, the English version, I think it was paragraph 6 was in B/C/S. I brought that to the attention of the Defence counsel and then I was provided with a copy with paragraph 6 with the English translation. But the English was one or two lines longer than the B/C/S, so I think that changed the page sequence of the following documents. So that may be what you're seeing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if we take out the original page which had paragraph 6 in B/C/S, then it should be okay, should it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because it doesn't match up, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. But the other paragraphs are identical, are they, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was only changing that B/C/S paragraph to English. Everything else remained the same as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In e-court it's final version, so I think that it's fine in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You take no objection to this statement, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We may have some difficulty, Mr. Lukic, with parts of paragraph 28, the references to Racak, because the trouble with these statements, although they're -- relate to the alleged bias of General DZ, determining whether they amount to bias could involve determining the rights and wrongs of what happened in Racak. But since there's no objection, we will admit the statement as it is, but bear in mind that that part in particular may have little relevance for the issues in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I also in this copy, but it may be the position is now different in the final version. [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit the statement, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can continue, Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and describe to us in a few sentences the relationship between the state security sector and public security sector?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Both the public security and state security sectors at that time existed within one single ministry, the ministry of the interior; however, these two sectors, both in the functional and personnel sense and also in the physical sense, were separated from each other. It was never the case in the history of the service, for as long as I have been a member of the service, that there was some kind of a relationship of subordination between the two. No. The two of them did their work separately, and there was this inter-sectoral cooperation, cooperation between these two sectors in terms of providing assistance, exchange of information. If something came to one sector and was actually within the jurisdiction of another sector, then the matter would be referred to the other sector, so there was this cooperation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear a question, I just heard "Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Kosovo, the premises in Pristina, the premises of the state security sector, were they in the same office as the MUP staff, or rather, the Pristina SUP?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. The organizational units of the state security sector in Pristina were located in a separate building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We saw that there was a lapse of one month between the time when the decision was issued on the 16th of June, 1998, to establish a staff, which is Exhibit P1505 and your arrival in Kosovo to the MUP staff. In your work did you hear that within that month David Gajic took part in the work of the MUP staff as a member of the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that. And in my previous evidence before the break I made a mistake in relation to Djinovic. I took Mr. Bonomy's question to mean what was Djinovic's position in the previous staff before the decision was made, in the staff headed by Colonel Aco Vesovic and that's why I said that he was deputy and I didn't pay attention to the actual question, but that's the essence of my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where was the MUP staff located in 1998 and early 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: The MUP staff was located in the building of the secretariat of the interior in Pristina and they used several offices in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was the building of the Pristina SUP bombed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: According to my recollection, the building was bombed in the night between the 28th and 29th of March, I'm not sure about the exact time, but I think it was then.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were any MUP staff members hurt at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On that occasion Dusko Adamovic was wounded, as was Vucurevic and Desimir Slovic. This is why these staff members were replaced by new members so that they stopped being members of the staff on the 1st of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were they replaced by other people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the new people came.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who came to the MUP staff to replace Dusko Adamovic, Radovan Vucurevic, and Desimir Slovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Milenko Arsenijevic came to replace Dusko Adamovic. Vucurevic was replaced by Petar Bogdanovic. And Slovic was replaced by Vojislav Gucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was Tomislav Blagojevic wounded on that occasion as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, slightly. And given that he had just arrived on the 15th of February to replace Novica Zdravkovic and he was only slightly wounded, he remained a member of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was anybody else sent to Kosovo and Metohija from the MUP seat without being a member of the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. Gagic came, I think his first name was Gvozden, Gvozden Gagic. He came from the criminal police administration, he came from ministry seat in Belgrade to assist with the activities aimed at suppressing the crimes, but he was not a member of the staff, he did not have a decision appointing him a member of the staff, he just came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the decision on establishing the staff on the -- issued on the 16th of June, 1998. We see that after Milorad Lukovic there is Zivko Trajkovic listed as a staff member. When you were a member of the staff of MUP, was Mr. Trajkovic a member at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. When I came down there, I didn't find him in the staff. As far as I know, he never did any work within the staff. I saw him at two or three meetings in the premises of the secretariat of the interior when meetings were held with all senior officers. So he was not a member of the staff. I'm describing the factual situation, even though here in the decision he's listed as having been a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work as member of the staff, did you learn whether Milorad Lukovic, Legija, and Zivko Trajkovic were members of the staff within that one-month period of time between the issuance of the decision on establishing the staff and your arrival in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about that, and I know that during the period of time while I was there they were within their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this decision you are not listed as a member of the staff, neither is Adamovic, Slovic, and later Arsenijevic, Bogdanovic, and Gucic. The people I mentioned, including yourself, were you members of the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The fact is that David Gajic, Lukovic, and Trajkovic were not members of the staff. Formally they were but practically they weren't. Formally speaking Adamovic, myself, Slovic, and others were not members of the staff and practically we were. So if you were to take as truth that Gajic, Trajkovic, and Lukic [as interpreted] were members of the staff and we were not, then you would simultaneously accept two untruths because, indeed, we were members of the staff and they were not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not Lukic but Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the second page, in the first paragraph, underneath the names that are listed it is stated that members of the staff, of the extended staff, will also include chiefs of the secretariats of internal affairs, centres, and branches of the RDB in the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo. These persons, were any of them members of the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were in charge of their organizational units, the units that they were responsible for. They would occasionally come to the senior staff meeting, but within the staff they had no tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us -- can you tell us what your position is about the following. In the personnel sense, did this decision reflect the actual situation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, and you can see this on the basis of my evidence, my previous evidence; partially yes and partially no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you something about the competencies of the staff. On the second page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do that, Mr. Lukic. Have you any explanation for this unutterable mess that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally don't have an explanation. I don't know why such a decision was issued, a decision that was not implemented, when other people were sent. I have no answer to this. It's -- it was up to the seniors at the ministry to decide this. I can't even explain why these people are listed down here, because as I've told you, not a single member of the state security sector could be in control of the members of the public security sector and vice versa, so I have no explanation. I don't understand why is it written down this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Mijatovic, let us now turn to the competencies of this staff, and would you please focus on Roman II --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My mistake again, sorry, there is one thing that thus remains unclear. You said a moment ago, Mr. Mijatovic, that those listed at the bottom as chiefs rather than by name were not members of the staff, but they occasionally came to senior staff meetings. Does that include the chiefs of the RDB department -- sorry, RDB branches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, chiefs of RDB branches came to those meetings once or twice when minister was there or one of his assistants sent by him to Kosovo and Metohija to hold meetings with people, to convey whatever they had to convey. But otherwise, they were not members of the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, Mr. Lukic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Roman II, that's what we're dealing with. We can see that in the decision on establishing the MUP staff, II, it says that it is the task of the staff to plan, organize, and manage the activities and use of the organizational units of the ministry as well as the units that were sent and attached aimed at suppressing terrorism in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. I'm asking you this now: Did the MUP staff plan the work of the organizational units of MUP in Kosovo and Metohija, the following organizational units: SUP, OUP, and police stations, these organizational units? Could you please explain to us what is a SUP, what is an OUP, and what is a police station.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I understood your question. The staff never planned, never organized, and never managed the work of the said organizational units for the simple reason that they functioned on the basis of the rule -- rules on organization of the units of the Ministry of the Interior. Secretariats of the interior are territorial organizational units of the ministry. As far as I remember, there were 33 of them, which means that all of these 33 secretariats covered part of the territory of the Republic of Serbia and all of them together covered the -- all of the territory of the Republic of Serbia. So they were in charge of organizing the work, planning it, managing it, and they were responsible to the minister for their work, chiefs of secretariats. Now when we're dealing with the departments of the interior, OUPs, and police stations, these are organizational units which are based on the territorial principle. They belong to the secretariat of the interior and they covered individual municipalities. And in some municipalities you had a department of the interior, and in smaller municipalities you had just police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've already answered my question whether the staff actually organized and managed the work of those organizational units, and now I would like to ask you whether the MUP staff planned anti-terrorist actions.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. The MUP staff did not plan any anti-terrorist actions, and as far as I know, no such plans were ever made, in fact, at the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did the MUP staff in the actual fact organize and manage anti-terrorist actions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, it did not plan them, it did not organize them, it did not manage or control them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the decision to establish the staff, in addition to not being reflective of the actual personnel situation in the field, was it actually ever implemented in practice, as indicated in II?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. The staff never did engage in those kind of tasks, which means that this part of this decision was never implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
