utterances.text: Did the MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija have people via which it would directly gather information on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. Based on the composition of the staff you could see that there was some dozen people there, two of which, Krdzic and Rajcic, were employees of the secretariat in Pristina and they carried out their regular work at the secretariat but would also occasionally do some work for the staff. So the number of persons there was insufficient in order to enable us to deal with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the analysts at the staff concealed or dropped some information from the staff reports that were sent to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that the analyst didn't do that. I can't claim that we checked every single report sent to Belgrade. We didn't check whether he included all of the elements. We mostly tried to put all the essential elements in those reports because we didn't want to burden them with details, but had he wanted to change anything in the report, had he wanted to omit something, it would have been impossible for him to do that, precisely because the same reports were sent to the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you something about your presence at the meetings outside of the MUP staff in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see P1468, please. Could we now turn to page 142 in the Serbian version and 157 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you found it, Mr. Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What date is this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: 22nd of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember attending this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I remember attending one meeting, since we can see in the minutes that I was there I guess that's the meeting that I attended. I couldn't tell you anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the nature of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing specific. They reported on some things, those who were in attendance. I wouldn't be able to tell you even who attended the meeting -- oh, it says here that Mr. Minic, Andjelkovic, and Lukic were not present, and then we can see the people who contributed something at the meeting, and based on what they said you can see that this was just a matter of providing information, just that, briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now could we turn to the content of this note here. It says here that Mr. Andjelkovic was not present, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yet, at the very same meeting, in the Serbian version that would be the next page, it is recorded that Mr. Andjelkovic participated in the debate. Could you explain this illogical thing in the minutes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I simply don't know, I cannot recall whether Andjelkovic was there or was not there. It says here that he was absent but also that he participated in the debate. So I couldn't really say anything about it. It was a long time ago and I can't really recall -- I can't be expected to recall who was present at that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've had problems trying to decipher the handwriting, but could you please be so kind and read what it says below your name and just above Mr. Andjelkovic's name, so that would be the intervention that is ascribed to you. So could you please read it but do it slowly so that the interpreters and everybody else in the courtroom is able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: "Our units entered" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that there is something further up there just below Colonel Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do apologise, you're right. "On the 22nd" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we go on, can we have the English version of this on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I said that it should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could you please start now.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. "On the 22nd of October, 1998, there" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand why some people here are obsessed with Mr. Sainovic, but I -- or rather, I do understand it, but I don't see why his name should be on the screen while we're talking about something else. Maybe somebody else needs it, but I don't. So could you please go further down in the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He happens to be on that page, Mr. Fila, and it's of no significance that it's there while we read something else, so let's please continue. Please continue, Mr. Andjelkovic -- Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please start reading now.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: "On the 22nd of October, 1998, there were several" -- I think it says "provocations but," the word is not finished here but I think it says "but no harm was caused to any of our personnel. Our units entered the S, village, of Glodjane," I suppose, "and the village of Jablanica without any major problems. During the day the police entered," it's really difficult to decipher the place names here, but these are obviously some place names, "and the police from Podujevo was in the village of," again we have some names of some villages, "and there were no problems."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to stop here for a moment. We're talking about the 22nd of October, 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any anti-terrorist actions going on at that time in light of the fact --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, the agreement was signed on the 16th of October, and from the time it was signed until the war started there were no anti-terrorist actions planned for that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So do you know what kind of police units we're talking about, police units entering some villages?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who made the minutes, I really don't know who was -- the drafter was, if it was somebody from the military then it doesn't really surprise me because in the army you often talk about units, commands, and so on and so forth. So even if we're talking about a dozen people or so, they would call it a unit, and in our parlance that would be a patrol, a reinforced patrol. So obviously the police entered the villages. So these are not units of any sort, these are not actions. These were just their -- they were just police doing their regular job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please go on reading now. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, the record again it says "minutes" where it should read "notes," that's 93, line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila, that happened on this occasion to be Mr. Lukic's choice of language I think, and he may have his own reasons for thinking that that's what they are. As I've said before, it's for us ultimately to look at all the evidence and decide what exactly they are. Please continue, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have misspoken. Could you please go on and read the next passage from the notes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: "Today a one or a strong, necessary" -- well, it's really difficult to read this handwriting, "a group, a patrol group" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Group.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: "Group arrived from Finland to check the situation in Kosovo and Metohija for the purpose of the exhumation of the bodies."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to stop you there. In this period of time, the 22nd of October, 1998, to the best of your recollection, was there any discussion about the arrival of a Finnish expert group that was supposed to exhume the bodies, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember whether it was at that time, but as far as I can remember, later on, yes, there was some discussion about the arrival of such a team, but that was after the incident in Racak, the incident in the village of Racak. And as for this period of time, I really can't say anything. I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please just finish reading until the end of this passage but do it slowly.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: "They were ordered to go" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "To be given ..."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: "To be given cases that are being processed."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please stop here. Does this wording actually mean that they were ordered that they be given something?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says. "They were ordered that they be given ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please read it to the end now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: "As regards the flags, the secretariats were ordered," the word is "nalog," "to place the Republic of Serbia flags on the MUP check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do those flags have anything to do with the forensic experts from Finland?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, no, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see that on page where we see the date, in Serbian that would be page 142, 157 in the English version, there right at the top you can see: Session or meeting of the ZK for KiM. You've explained to us what the nature of this meeting was. Now I would like to ask you the following. At that time, did you know the term "Joint Command"? Had you heard of it at any point?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I did hear that term being mentioned, but when I attended this meeting I did not understand it to be a meeting of the Joint Command. And I did not consider myself to be attending a meeting of any kind of command, in fact, because everybody said whatever it was that they had to say and then we all went our separate ways. There were no obligations, no tasks of any kind. I wasn't able to see who was in charge, who were just bit players. I was not a member of any command, but I just presented my report. That's the only thing I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So to the best of your recollection, that was the only time that you attended a meeting of this sort?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't recall having attended any other meeting apart from this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you don't appear to remember anything that happened at this one; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I was asked whether I had attended any other meetings apart from this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but did you attend this one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't remember. I know that I attended one meeting, I don't know whether it was this one because I can't recall the date, but I guess I did attend it because it is recorded here in the notebook. I'm sure that I attended one meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can't remember any of this subject matter that we've been looking at so far, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what you mean, what subject matter you mean. I said what I had to say, what I was aware of. I don't know whether you mean those meetings or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would like to know what it is you remember anyone, including yourself, saying at the meeting that you attended.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, well it's recorded in the notes or the minutes. It is difficult for me to actually read it, to see who said what. The handwriting is really hard to decipher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but you're recorded as having reported on a monitoring group from Finland coming to investigate the situation in Kosovo and to exhume bodies, and you apparently don't remember that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't remember really because I know that the Finnish team was there after the incident in Racak because they were dealing with the events in Racak, but I don't recall for the previous period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know that this has got nothing with Racak, it's before that. And there's a reference to the Minister Andjelkovic talking about setting up mixed local police in Kijevo. Do you remember that subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall that topic at that meeting, but I do recall about the local police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, as far as I'm concerned, Mr. Lukic, speaking for myself, the witness doesn't remember being at this meeting. Perhaps it will become clearer, but at the moment that's how I understand it. He hasn't identified anything that he remembers occurring at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will not be asking you any more questions regarding the notes. I will ask you something about the Joint Command. The MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija, did it ever receive any orders, "nalog," from a body called the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the MUP staff, did it have any obligations vis-a-vis a body that would be called the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what were the regulations for the work of the organizational units of the Ministry of the Interior in Kosovo and Metohija? We've already discussed that --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: We've already discussed that. That was done by the rules of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, in 1998 and 1999 was it possible for a body that would be outside of the structure of the MUP and the Army of Yugoslavia to assume command or control of the units within those two bodies?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that this was done and in my opinion it couldn't have been done because it would have disrupted the chain of command that is based on rules. I can't see how a new body could be established to disrupt this chain of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the course of your work, were you ever aware of the existence of a Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, precisely for these reasons. I did not see a single order, "nalog," or did I know of any obligation in terms of providing return information to a command like that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view what would a command have to have at least?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, somebody would have to establish this command. The command would have to have a person in charge, regardless of whether it's called a commander or whatever. It would have to -- this commander would have to have his deputies, assistants, his co-workers, they would have to have their command post premises that they would use, a system of communications, telephones through which they would communicate, security in particular at that time in Kosovo and Metohija. Assignments would have to be issued by that command and there would have to be feedback information as to what had been done. I am not aware of any such thing. Quite simply I never felt anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to ask a very banal question. Did you know a telephone number that would be linked to a Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: At the same time, I do not remember any single number, but I know that on our list of telephones, because we did have a list of telephones that we communicated with in the ministry and down there in Kosovo, but we quite certainly did not have the telephone number of a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask for 6D1323 to be called up in e-court once again, and I will just ask Mr. Mijatovic to read out a particular point to us from this rule -- instructions, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, this is the one you objected to. It seems that one point is going to be asked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess I will wait and see what the question is and see if I want to raise something about it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all I would like to ask you, Mr. Mijatovic, whether it is natural for there to be coordinating activities among different state organs at different levels.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: I find that to be quite natural and that was what was done at all levels. It is natural for ministries of the interior to communicate, or rather, the Ministry of the Interior and the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. It is natural that they all together communicate with other ministers from the government, with the Speaker of the Assembly and so on and so forth, and also at lower levels, it is only natural, in Kosovska Mitrovica, Prizren, never mind, it is only natural that the chief of SUP should communicate with the commander of the brigade, with the president of the municipality, the head of the district to exchange information and so on and so forth. I do apologise, it seems to me that I am speaking a bit too fast. So I find that to be quite natural. After all, I don't know how they would function if they were only confined to their own shell, if they would clam up, I find that to be unnatural.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. I'm sorry, 6D1323 is what we are dealing with now, and could we look at page 2.9. Since this document has not been translated, I kindly ask you to read this paragraph slowly.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: May I start? "The chief of the secretariat of the interior, in addition to urgent information mentioned in items 7 and 8 of these instructions shall also ensure urgent information of organs of municipalities and cities and chiefs of districts about events and occurrences mentioned in points 55 through 62, 73 through 75, and 104 through 107 of the list of information and reporting."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please read the next subparagraph of this same paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: "Urgent information mentioned in paragraph 1 of this item provides for the sending of urgent information to the Assembly of the municipality or city and the chief of the district at the same time when it is being sent to the organizational unit in the seat of the ministry that is in charge."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe that we don't need the rest. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the chiefs of the SUPs, that is to say the secretariat of the interior, are they duty-bound to provide information to the civilian authorities as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We see here that in addition to it being necessary, they also have the obligation to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about the minister of the interior, for instance, the republican minister, is it his duty to report to the Assembly of the republic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is his duty according to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe we should ask Mr. Hannis if there's any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let sleeping dogs lie, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if we're going to go any more, I'll re-raise my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I anticipate that, but I think your silence spoke volumes there. Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we are going to leave this document aside and we're going to move on to what the situation was like on the eve of the war. Could you please focus on that particular period. What were the comments being made in February 1999 in the environment that you lived and worked in in relation to the Rambouillet negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not only in the environment where I was at the time, but generally speaking in Serbia, as far as I know from my contacts with friends and relatives, in view of how the negotiations in Rambouillet were progressing, in all likelihood the negotiations did not seem to be successful and probably an attack would be launched against our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The MUP of the Republic of Serbia, did it take all necessary measures before and after the negotiations in Rambouillet for the signed agreements with the OSCE to be observed fully?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. There were quite a few meetings, quite a few documents were being sent out into the field in order to have maximum measures taken so that the agreement could be observed fully. Because we knew, although we had all assessed that this agreement was rather unfavourable to our country, but it was there and the state leadership wanted to avoid having the country bombed. That is why, as far as I know, from all levels maximum efforts were made to observe the agreement, even suffering certain consequences during that time. Nevertheless, everything was done. However, as we all know, this did not yield any results and ultimately we were bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time what kind of a danger came from Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: From Macedonia there was the danger of the land forces of NATO entering Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Due to this kind of situation, did anyone from the MUP leadership go to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up in e-court P1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please look at pages 2 to 4. In English 2 to 6. Did you manage?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what kind of a document this is?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: These are the minutes from the meeting held at the MUP staff in Pristina on the 17th of March, 1999, with the senior staff attended by the minister and his closest associates. When I refer to the senior staff, I'm referring both to public security and state security, including chiefs of both sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In principle, what did the minister convey to police members gathered there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in principle, as always, he provided the assessment of the work, provided guide-lines for future work, for upcoming tasks, this is something that was mostly done during all meetings. And naturally he said that should the country be attacked, it will defend itself using all forces available to it so that we had to be ready for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now would you please turn to page 1, fifth line from above on page 1, under the name of General Sreten Lukic it says as follows: "The staff planned to carry this out when this is ordered, three sweeping actions aimed at getting rid of the terrorists in Dragobilje, Drenica, for that task we prepared 4.000 policemen from operational pursuit group and about 900 from reserve forces" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you gave us the wrong page for that reference, Mr. Lukic. You said page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In B/C/S, sorry. It's page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ah, right. Thanks. 4.000 and around -- 4.000 policemen and then 70 from the operative --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but 70 from the operative pursuit group, which hasn't been reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I read it, yeah, okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mijatovic, does this discuss creation of plans or something else?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV MIJATOVIC
utterances.text: As I have said in my evidence earlier, the MUP staff in Pristina did not draft any plans for any anti-terrorist action whatsoever. This pertained to three locations, and this activity was planned by the Pristina Corps. In order for them to plan this, they had to receive from the staff the information on the units participating in this action; and based on that, General Lukic informed the minister about the three actions which were certainly not planned by the staff. As far as I remember, these three actions were not carried out until the beginning of the bombing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This minute is the 17th of February; is that correct, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For some reason I wrote March down, it may say March somewhere, but it is February.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could we now see in e-court Exhibit 6D269.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the next set of questions you would need to look at the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I think we ran out of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We can interrupt at this stage. Mr. Mijatovic, we have to terminate our proceedings for the day at this point. That means that you have to return tomorrow to continue with your evidence; that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I've understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I expect you may not complete your evidence tomorrow but also have to return on Thursday. Between now and your completing giving evidence here, it is vitally important that you have no communication with anyone at all about any aspect of the evidence in this case, either your evidence or that of any other person in the case. You can talk to whoever you like about whatever you like except the evidence in this case. Now, please bear that in mind and now leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 13th day of February, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.30 p.m.,
